lesson.title: Selling the War: George Creel and the Birth of American Propaganda
lesson.summary: To rally a divided public behind the war effort, Wilson created the Committee on Public Information under journalist George Creel, an unprecedented government propaganda operation whose posters, films, and volunteer speakers sometimes fueled intolerance toward German Americans and antiwar dissenters.
lesson.body:
When the United States entered World War I in April 1917, American public opinion was far from unanimous in its support. Many German Americans, Irish Americans, socialists, and pacifists harbored real doubts or outright opposition to the war, and the Wilson administration worried that without a unified home front, the ambitious mobilization effort described in the previous chapter would falter. Wilson's answer was to create a government agency dedicated entirely to shaping public opinion.

By executive order on April 13, 1917, Wilson established the Committee on Public Information, commonly known as the CPI, and placed it under the leadership of George Creel, a muckraking journalist with a talent for persuasion. The CPI became one of the first large-scale, government-run propaganda operations in American history. It commissioned artists to design memorable war posters, funded short films promoting the war effort, distributed millions of pamphlets, and organized a corps of roughly 75,000 volunteer speakers known as the Four-Minute Men, who delivered brief patriotic speeches in movie theaters, churches, and public gatherings across the country.

The CPI proved remarkably effective at generating enthusiasm for the war and boosting sales of the Liberty Bonds discussed earlier. But its success came with a serious cost. The campaign often blurred the line between patriotism and intolerance, stoking exaggerated fears of German spies and saboteurs. Anti-German sentiment spread quickly during the war years, leading many schools to drop German language instruction, prompting some communities to rename sauerkraut liberty cabbage and hamburger the liberty sandwich, and casting suspicion on German-language newspapers and German American communities generally.

By encouraging Americans to see loyalty and dissent in stark, simple terms, the CPI helped create a climate in which questioning the war could be viewed as nearly treasonous. That climate set the stage directly for the next chapter, in which the federal government moved from persuading Americans to support the war toward legally punishing those who criticized it.
